content: The Aqua Detox device is marketed as a tool for detoxification. It operates by immersing an individual’s feet in a saline solution while an electrical current is passed through the bath. The device is said to be based on the research of Royal Rife. However, it has faced criticism for misleading consumers. Variants of the device are sold under numerous brand names, partly because the original manufacturer provides in-house web design services to resellers. As of October 15, 2006, the Aqua Detox brand became part of a new parent company called The Agenda Group. Although the manufacturer does not explicitly claim that Aqua Detox can treat or cure diseases, the company Aqua Detox International was the subject of a British Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) ruling on April 6, 2005. The ASA challenged the use of user testimonials that implied the device’s efficacy in treating serious diseases, as well as the general effectiveness of the device. Both complaints were upheld. The company did not address the device’s efficacy but agreed to remove misleading testimonials from its advertisements. One marketer, Miracle Beauty, claims that the color of the water in the footbath indicates which areas of the body have allegedly been cleansed of toxins. For example, black is said to represent the liver, orange the joints, and green the gallbladder. However, Aqua Detox machines use iron electrodes that corrode during use, producing rust that turns the water brown when the saline solution is electrolyzed. Variations in water color can be attributed to the amount of salt added and differences in the composition of the electrodes. An experiment using saltwater and a car battery demonstrated that the water changes color regardless of whether feet are present in the bath. Furthermore, the composition of the analyzed water was the same in both cases, with or without feet. Critics, such as Stephen Barrett, argue that the process is merely electrolysis, or the rusting of the electrodes (in the case of iron), and that the color change is being exploited by manufacturers to deceive consumers. The Aqua Detox device has not been evaluated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Marketing materials for the product include a disclaimer stating that it is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.
